Volt and ohm in SI base units?
column2: V = W/A = kg·m²/(s³·A); Ω = V/A = kg·m²/(s³·A²). Every electrical unit is mechanics plus the ampere.

column1: Energy units: eV, Wh, kWh in joules?
column2: 1 eV = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ J (exact); 1 Wh = 3600 J; 1 kWh = 3.6 MJ. Battery energy (Wh) = Ah × V.

column1: What does an accelerometer at rest on a table read? In free fall?
column2: +1 g upward at rest (the table's push per unit mass); zero in free fall. It measures specific force, acceleration minus gravity.

column1: Work–energy theorem?
column2: Net work equals the change in kinetic energy: \(\int F\,dx = \tfrac12mv_2^2 - \tfrac12mv_1^2\), from \(a = v\,dv/dx\).

column1: Mechanical power, linear and rotational?
column2: \(P = Fv\) and \(P = \tau\omega\) (ω in rad/s; ω = 2π·rpm/60). The twin of \(P = vi\). 1 hp ≈ 745.7 W.

column1: Impulse–momentum theorem, and why foam protects a dropped device?
column2: \(\int F\,dt = \Delta p\). The momentum change is fixed by the impact speed; foam stretches the stopping time, so force and deceleration fall in proportion.

column1: Half-sine shock pulse: peak versus average deceleration?
column2: Peak = (π/2) × average = (π/2)·v/Δt. A 1.5 m drop (5.42 m/s) stopped in 0.2 ms: about 2765 g average, 4344 g peak.

column1: Simple harmonic oscillator: frequency and energy?
column2: \(\omega_0 = \sqrt{k_s/m}\); \(K + U = \tfrac12k_sA^2\) constant; each store averages half; peak speed \(A\omega_0\), peak acceleration \(A\omega_0^2\).

column1: Damped oscillator: ζ, Q and decay rate?
column2: \(\zeta = b/(2\sqrt{k_sm})\), \(Q = 1/(2\zeta) = m\omega_0/b\), \(\alpha = b/(2m) = \omega_0/(2Q)\). Amplitude falls by e in Q/π cycles.

column1: Q as an energy ratio?
column2: \(Q = 2\pi\) × (energy stored)/(energy lost per cycle), exact as Q grows large. Q = 10,000 loses 2π/10,000 of its energy per cycle.

column1: Force–voltage analogy?
column2: F ↔ v, velocity ↔ i, x ↔ q, m ↔ L, b ↔ R, 1/k_s ↔ C. Springs in series (one force) map to capacitors in parallel.

column1: Accelerometer sensitivity and bandwidth?
column2: Deflection \(x = a/\omega_0^2\) below resonance: 15.53 nm per g at 4 kHz. With Q = 0.707 the bandwidth is \(f_0\). Four times the bandwidth costs sixteen times the deflection.

column1: Thermomechanical (Brownian) noise of a proof mass?
column2: Force noise \(4kTb\) (twin of 4kTR) gives \(a_n = \sqrt{4kT\omega_0/(mQ)}\): 35 µg/√Hz for 5 µg, 4 kHz, Q = 0.707. Lower it with more mass or higher Q.

column1: Equipartition for a spring?
column2: \(\tfrac12k_s\overline{x^2} = \tfrac12kT\), so \(x_{\text{rms}} = \sqrt{kT/k_s}\), independent of mass and damping: 64 pm for 1 N/m at 300 K. The mechanical kT/C.

column1: Why do watch crystals run at 32,768 Hz?
column2: 32,768 = 2¹⁵: fifteen divide-by-two stages give exactly 1 Hz.

column1: Resonator frequency by dimensions?
column2: \(\omega_0 \propto (1/L)\sqrt{E/\rho}\): shrinking a structure tenfold raises its frequency tenfold. √(E/ρ) ≈ 8.5 km/s in silicon.

column1: Elementary charge, and electrons per coulomb?
column2: e = 1.602176634×10⁻¹⁹ C exactly (2019 SI); 1 C = 6.242×10¹⁸ electrons. 1 mA for 1 s moves 6.24×10¹⁵ electrons.

column1: Coulomb's law?
column2: F = q₁q₂/(4πε₀r²) along the line joining the charges; like signs repel. k_e = 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.988×10⁹ N·m²/C².

column1: Electric field of a point charge, and its definition?
column2: E = F/q (V/m = N/C). Point charge: E = k_e q/r², radially away from a positive charge, toward a negative one.

column1: Superposition in electrostatics?
column2: The total field is the vector sum of each charge's field; for continuous charge, integrate dE = k_e dq/r² with components. Use symmetry to kill components first.

column1: Field of an infinite line charge λ at distance r?
column2: E = λ/(2πε₀r), falling as 1/r. A finite rod looks infinite close in (r ≪ length) and like a point charge far away.

column1: Field of an infinite sheet σ? Of two opposite sheets?
column2: One sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀), independent of distance. Two plates ±σ: E = σ/ε₀ between, zero outside (the capacitor field).

column1: On-axis field of a ring (charge Q, radius R)?
column2: E_z = k_e Q z/(z² + R²)^{3/2}: zero at the center, peaks at z = R/√2, and becomes k_e Q/z² far away.

column1: Electric dipole: moment, far field, torque, energy?
column2: p = qd from − to +. Far field ∝ 1/r³ (2k_e p/r³ on axis, k_e p/r³ on the bisector). Uniform field: τ = pE sin θ, U = −pE cos θ, no net force.

column1: Why does a dipole field fall as 1/r³?
column2: The two charges' 1/r² fields nearly cancel; the leftover is their difference, (d/r) times smaller, so k_e q/r² × d/r ∝ p/r³.

column1: Kinetic energy and speed after accelerating through V?
column2: qV = ½mv², so v = √(2qV/m). An electron through 1 V gains 1 eV = 1.602×10⁻¹⁹ J; through 2 kV it reaches 2.65×10⁷ m/s (0.088c).

column1: Exit angle of a charged beam through deflection plates?
column2: tan θ = V_d L/(2 V_a d), independent of the particle's charge and mass, because both acceleration and deflection scale with q/m.

column1: Breakdown fields of air and thermal SiO₂?
column2: Air ≈ 3 MV/m (3 kV/mm); thermal SiO₂ > 10 MV/cm, about 1000× more. A 1.2 nm oxide at 1 V carries 8.3 MV/cm.

column1: Human-body model (HBM) ESD network?
column2: 100 pF discharged through 1.5 kΩ (JS-001): peak 0.667 A per kV, τ = 150 ns. 2 kV gives 1.333 A peak and 200 µJ stored.

column1: IEC 61000-4-2 system-level ESD network, versus HBM?
column2: 150 pF through 330 Ω, τ ≈ 50 ns: at 8 kV about 24 A peak against 5.3 A for HBM. A chip's HBM rating does not cover a connector's system-level test.

column1: Industry-recommended ESD qualification targets?
column2: 1 kV HBM and 250 V CDM are safe with basic factory controls (Industry Council, JEP155/JEP157); below about 500 V HBM or 125 V CDM, advanced controls are needed.

column1: CDM versus HBM?
column2: HBM: a charged person discharges into a pin (slow, 100 pF/1.5 kΩ). CDM (JS-002): the charged device itself discharges through one pin to ground, a sub-nanosecond, high-current event.

column1: Electric flux through a flat surface in a uniform field?
column2: Φ = EA cos θ (V·m), θ between E and the surface normal: maximum face-on, zero edge-on. On a closed surface the normal points outward.

column1: Gauss's law?
column2: ∮ E·n̂ dA = Q_enc/ε₀: net flux out of any closed surface equals the enclosed charge over ε₀. 1 nC gives 112.9 V·m.

column1: Why does Gauss's law need the inverse-square law?
column2: Flux through a sphere is E·4πr²; it is independent of r only if E ∝ 1/r². Experiments confirm the exponent is 2 to parts in 10¹⁶.

column1: Do charges outside a Gaussian surface affect the field on it?
column2: Yes: they change E at every point, but their net flux through the closed surface is zero, so they drop out of Gauss's law.

column1: When is Gauss's law useful for finding E?
column2: Only with symmetry (spherical, cylindrical, planar), where a surface has E constant and perpendicular on part and parallel on the rest. A cube, a finite rod or a dipole has none.

column1: Field of a uniformly charged solid sphere? Of a thin shell?
column2: Solid: E = k_eQr/R³ inside (linear), k_eQ/r² outside. Shell: zero everywhere inside, k_eQ/r² outside.

column1: Field of a coaxial line with ±λ?
column2: E = λ/(2πε₀r) between the conductors, largest at the inner conductor; zero outside, since the enclosed charge is zero.

column1: Pillbox result for an infinite sheet, and for a slab of density ρ?
column2: Sheet: E = σ/(2ε₀). Slab of thickness t: E = ρx/ε₀ inside (zero at the midplane), ρt/(2ε₀) outside.

column1: Properties of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium?
column2: E = 0 inside the metal; net charge on the surface; field just outside perpendicular with magnitude σ/ε₀; an empty cavity is field-free.

column1: Why is the field outside a conductor σ/ε₀, not σ/(2ε₀)?
column2: An isolated sheet sends half its flux each way; on a conductor the other charges cancel the field inside the metal, so all the flux goes outward.

column1: A charge sits inside a neutral metal shell. Is the outside shielded?
column2: No: −q gathers on the inner wall and +q on the outer surface, so outside sees q. Grounding the shell drains the outer charge and shields both ways.

column1: Why does charge crowd onto sharp points?
column2: Connected conductors share one potential, kQ/R, so σ ∝ 1/R: small radii carry high σ and high field. Sharp points break down first (lightning rods, corona).

column1: Gauss's law in a material, and the interface rule?
column2: Use ε = ε_rε₀ with free charge: ∮εE·dA = Q_free. With no free interface charge, ε₁E₁n = ε₂E₂n (E in Si is 1/3 of E in SiO₂).

column1: pn-junction depletion region by Gauss's law?
column2: Slabs −qN_A (width x_p) and +qN_D (width x_n) with N_Ax_p = N_Dx_n. Triangular field peaking at the junction: E_max = qN_Dx_n/ε_s. The light side holds most of the width.

column1: Self-capacitance touch sensing in one line?
column2: A finger adds C_F = ε_rε₀A/d in parallel with the pad's parasitic C_P; typical C_F ≈ 0.1 pF on ≈ 33 pF, so the electronics must resolve well under 1% (Infineon AN85951, as of Nov 2026).

column1: Why is the electrostatic field conservative, and what does that buy?
column2: A point charge's field is radial, so work depends only on start and end distances; superposition extends this to any static charges. ∮E·dl = 0, so voltage (a potential function) is well defined: KVL.

column1: Potential from field, and field from potential?
column2: V_b − V_a = −∫_a^b E·dl (V falls along E); E = −∇V. A uniform field E over distance d drops V by Ed.

column1: Potential of a point charge, and of several?
column2: V = k_e q/r (zero at infinity). Potentials add as plain numbers: V = Σ k_e q_i/r_i, no vector components.

column1: Can V be zero where E is not, or E zero where V is not?
column2: Yes to both: midway between ±q, V = 0 but E is strong; at a charged ring's center, E = 0 but V = k_eQ/R. Field is the slope of potential, not its level.

column1: Why is a conductor an equipotential, and where is its field strongest?
column2: E = 0 inside means no work moving through it. An isolated sphere has E = V/R at its surface, so sharp (small-radius) parts carry the strongest field at a given voltage.

column1: Capacitance of parallel plates, a coax and a sphere?
column2: εA/d; 2πεℓ/ln(b/a); isolated sphere 4πε₀R (1 mm sphere ≈ 0.111 pF, the Earth ≈ 0.709 mF).

column1: Capacitors in series and parallel?
column2: Parallel: C = C₁ + C₂ (same V, charges add). Series: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ (same Q, voltages add); the smallest capacitor takes the largest voltage.

column1: Best coax inner radius for breakdown with fixed outer radius b?
column2: V_max = E_bd a ln(b/a) is largest at b/a = e, giving V_max = E_bd b/e.

column1: How does a dielectric raise capacitance?
column2: Its aligned dipoles leave bound charge at its faces that partly cancels the free charge; E falls to σ_f/(ε_rε₀), so V falls and C rises by ε_r = 1 + χ.

column1: Electric displacement D and its boundary rule?
column2: D = ε₀E + P = εE; ∮D·dA = Q_free. With no free interface charge, normal D is continuous: ε₁E₁n = ε₂E₂n.

column1: Equivalent oxide thickness (EOT)?
column2: EOT = Σ t_i × 3.9/ε_r,i: the SiO₂ thickness with the same C per area. 2 nm HfO₂ (ε_r 25) = 0.312 nm. Physical thickness sets tunneling; EOT sets capacitance.

column1: Layered dielectrics: which layer has the strongest field?
column2: The lowest-permittivity layer: D is the same in every layer, so E = D/ε is largest where ε is smallest (e.g. the SiO₂ interface layer under HfO₂).

column1: Energy stored in a capacitor, and where it lives?
column2: U = Q²/2C = ½CV² = ½QV, stored in the field at density u = ½εE². Switching C through V each cycle costs dynamic power αCV²f.

column1: Energy lost when two equal capacitors share charge?
column2: Half the initial energy, dissipated in the connecting resistance whatever its value (with none, radiated). DRAM reads are charge sharing: ΔV = (V_cell − V_BL)·C_s/(C_s + C_BL).

column1: Electrostatic pressure, and the chuck force?
column2: p = ½ε₀E² = D²/2ε₀ in a vacuum or air gap (≈ 40 Pa at 3 MV/m). A chuck's F = ε₀SV²/[2(g + l/ε_r)²] → D²S/2ε₀ at zero gap: 36.9 N for a 200 mm wafer at 1 kV on 0.54 mm alumina.

column1: MLCC classes and DC-bias loss?
column2: C0G (class 1): 0 ± 30 ppm/°C, no DC-bias loss. X5R/X7R (class 2, BaTiO₃, ε_r 1000–4000): ±15% over temperature, and lose capacitance with DC bias (Murata: 100 µF X5R at 1.8 V ≈ 90 µF; Y5V ≈ 60 µF).

column1: Current density in terms of carriers?
column2: J = nqv_d (A/m²); current I is the flux of J through a surface. For electrons J points opposite to their drift.

column1: Drift speed of 1 A in 1 mm² of copper, and why signals are still fast?
column2: About 74 µm/s (n = 8.49×10²⁸ m⁻³). The wire is already full of electrons; the signal travels with the field at a large fraction of c.

column1: Continuity equation and KCL?
column2: ∇·J = −∂ρ/∂t: outflow equals the rate of charge loss. At a node storing no charge, currents in = currents out (KCL); with capacitance, C dV/dt = net inflow.

column1: Drude model in one line?
column2: m dv/dt = −eE − mv/τ → v_d = −(eτ/m)E, so J = σE with σ = ne²τ/m = neµ: Ohm's law from random collisions.

column1: Copper's Drude numbers?
column2: ρ 1.68 µΩ·cm, σ 5.95×10⁷ S/m, τ ≈ 25 fs, µ ≈ 44 cm²/V·s, λ = v_Fτ ≈ 39 nm (Fermi speed 1.57×10⁶ m/s).

column1: Why does copper conduct better than silicon despite lower mobility?
column2: σ = neµ: copper has ~10¹² times more carriers than pure silicon, which outweighs silicon's ~30× higher mobility.

column1: Silicon conductivity and mobilities?
column2: σ = e(nµₙ + pµₚ); lightly doped Si µₙ ≈ 1400, µₚ ≈ 470 cm²/V·s. Pure Si ≈ 3×10⁵ Ω·cm; 10¹⁵ donors/cm³ ≈ 4.5 Ω·cm.

column1: Resistance from geometry, and sheet resistance?
column2: R = ρL/A. For a film of thickness t, R_s = ρ/t (Ω/□) and R = R_s·(L/W). 1 oz PCB copper: 34 µm, ≈ 0.49 mΩ/□.

column1: Temperature dependence of copper's resistance?
column2: ρ = ρ₀[1 + α(T − 20 °C)] with α = 0.00393 /°C: +31% from 20 to 100 °C. Resistance doubles as a thermometer.

column1: Why do narrow copper wires get worse?
column2: Below the ~40 nm mean free path, surface and grain-boundary scattering raise ρ, and a 2–3 nm barrier/liner steals area (30% of a 20 × 40 nm line).

column1: Joule heating, globally and locally?
column2: P = IV = I²R = V²/R; per volume p = J·E = σE² = ρJ². Heat concentrates where current crowds.

column1: Electromigration?
column2: High current density pushes metal atoms along the electron flow, forming voids and hillocks; it caps DC current density (ITRS 2015 projected ~0.3 MA/cm² for minimum Cu lines by 2026), mainly a power-grid problem.

column1: Distributed RC wire delay?
column2: t₅₀ ≈ 0.38RC with R = rL and C = cL, so delay ∝ L². A lumped RC (0.69RC) overestimates; repeaters make long-wire delay linear in L.

column1: What happens to wire RC when all cross-section dimensions shrink by s?
column2: Resistance per length rises by 1/s²; capacitance per length stays about the same. Local wires keep pace; global wires slow every node.

column1: Why move power delivery to the wafer's back side?
column2: Thick, short backside wires cut IR drop and free front-side tracks for signals. Intel ships PowerVia on 18A (Panther Lake, late 2025); TSMC's A16 Super Power Rail was shown for 2027 (as of Nov 2026).

column1: Magnetic force on a moving charge?
column2: F = qv × B, perpendicular to v and B, magnitude |q|vB sin θ. It does no work: it bends paths, never changes speed.

column1: Orbit radius and cyclotron frequency?
column2: r = mv/(|q|B); f_c = |q|B/(2πm), independent of speed (28.0 GHz/T for electrons). Motion along B is unaffected: helices.

column1: How does an implanter's analyzer magnet pick one ion species?
column2: Ions accelerated through V circle with r = √(2mV/q)/B, so radius grows as √m; a slit passes one mass (e.g. ¹¹B⁺ at 9.55 cm for 10 keV in 0.5 T).

column1: Velocity selector and E×B drift?
column2: Crossed E and B pass only v = E/B undeflected. A charge released in crossed fields drifts at E/B along E × B, whatever its charge or mass.

column1: Force on a current, and torque on a coil?
column2: F = IL × B. A coil has moment m = NIA (A·m²); torque τ = m × B, energy U = −m·B: the DC motor principle.

column1: Biot–Savart law and the long-wire field?
column2: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl × r̂/r². Long wire: B = µ₀I/(2πr) = 20 µT at 1 cm per ampere (Earth ≈ 50 µT). Loop center: µ₀I/(2R).

column1: Force between parallel wires?
column2: F/L = µ₀I₁I₂/(2πd): attract for same-direction currents, repel for opposite. Goes as current squared: 20 N/m at 1 kA, 1 cm; 2000 N/m at 10 kA.

column1: Ampère's law and its standard results?
column2: ∮B·dl = µ₀I_enc. Inside a wire B ∝ r; solenoid B = µ₀nI; toroid B = µ₀NI/(2πr) confined to the core; coax B = 0 outside.

column1: Gauss's law for magnetism?
column2: ∮B·dA = 0: no magnetic monopoles, so field lines close on themselves.

column1: Hall voltage and what it measures?
column2: V_H = IB/(nqt). Sign → carrier type (electrons vs holes); size → density n; with resistivity, mobility µ = |R_H|σ.

column1: Why are Hall sensors semiconductors, not metals?
column2: V_H ∝ 1/n: copper's 8.5×10²⁸ m⁻³ gives sub-µV; silicon at 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ gives mV from mA.

column1: How does a Hall current sensor reject stray fields?
column2: Two Hall plates see the conductor's field with opposite signs but a uniform stray field with the same sign; subtracting doubles the signal and cancels the stray field.

column1: B, H, M and relative permeability?
column2: B = µ₀(H + M); ∮H·dl = I_free. Linear materials: B = µ_rµ₀H, µ_r ≈ 1 for most, hundreds to tens of thousands for ferromagnets.

column1: Core saturation, and why gaps help?
column2: Above B_s the core adds nothing and inductance collapses. A gap g adds g/µ₀ to the magnetic path, raising saturation current many-fold at the cost of inductance per turn. Ferrite (N87) B_s: 0.49 T at 25 °C, 0.39 T at 100 °C.

column1: Soft vs hard magnetic materials?
column2: Soft (ferrite, Si steel, powder cores): narrow B–H loops, low loss, used in inductors and transformers. Hard (NdFeB, ferrite magnets): wide loops, stay magnetized, used in motors and speakers.

column1: What stores a bit in MRAM?
column2: A magnetic tunnel junction: its tunneling resistance is lower when the two magnetic layers are parallel. Embedded MRAM is in production at 28, 22 and 16 nm foundry processes (as of Nov 2026).
